surfaces.part: open interior floor with rubble, seen from above

answer.evidence: Rows 10-13 show light wall tops, and rows 14-31 show an open interior floor with rubble, which is evidence (d). Rows 32-35 form a light front wall top band with a front-edge line at row 35, followed by a darker row at 36. Below that, the front face runs from about row 39 to row 95 and holds two storeys of window holes plus a dark doorway. The collapsed corner on the right is drawn as a sloped rubble heap. The silhouette is a uniform 80 px wide, so no side face is drawn. The building has a clear top region and a tall front face, so it reads as three-quarter.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate has 16 visible tones per tile against 12 and 10 for the references, so its density is at or above theirs. Its near-flat coverage is 8% against 0%, which is slightly higher but small. In the picture the concrete walls and floor carry speckle, stain and crack variation. The rubble ramp has scattered brick-red and grey chunks, and green vegetation clumps add more variation. Only 18% of the dark edge pixels are neutral, so the outlines lean tinted (dark grey-brown or blue-grey beside the concrete), not a uniform black sticker line. The concrete ramp has about 5 lightness steps, one fewer than the roof and wall ramps of the references. The darkest window holes and the collapsed-corner void are fairly flat, but they are small areas of deliberate shadow. A careful artist would accept it next to the references without it looking thinner or flatter.

Near-flat coverage is 8%, against 0% for both references, so there are a few flat patches, but they are small. Only 18% of dark edge pixels are near-neutral, so the outlines carry a tint and read as dark material tone, not a black sticker line.
